  standard library and the examples call nothing deprecated, and `npm test`
  fails the day one of them does. **Nothing is deprecated today**: band NL7xxx
  holds only the retired NL7001 (`Arena.release` and `Arena.reset`) and NL7002
  (`--unchecked-indexing`'s sites), whose constructs were removed before 1.0
  rather than kept behind a warning (`tests/wordings/unreachable.txt`).
- **`--json`** prints every diagnostic as one JSON object per line on stdout,
  `{"file","line","column","endLine","endColumn","severity","code","message"}`
  (1-based, end exclusive; syntax errors carry a `syntax error: ` prefix in
  `message`), nothing else on stdout and nothing on stderr, with the same exit
  code. `severity` is `"error"` for every error, `"performance"` for a
  WP15 §8 warning, `"portability"` for a WP33 one and `"deprecation"` for a
  deprecated call, which is the field a tool filters on; `code` is the stable
  identifier for the rule (`NL1013`, `NL2231`, ...) and is the field to key on,
  because the prose may improve between releases and the code may not. A
  diagnostic in a dependency's source — a module resolved into a package
  other than the root and the standard library — adds `"package"`, the
  package's name, after `message` (and before a `fix`), and its human report
  adds a line under the excerpt, `` = note: this is in the dependency
  `pkg_broken` 0.3.1, not in this program's own source `` (WP21 S3,
  `tests/link/package_dependency_error`). A
  failure with no source position — an unusable C toolchain, an internal
  compiler error, a bad `-o` layout — is `{"severity","code","message"}`. Two
  optional keys follow `message`, each a list of edits
  `[{"line","column","endLine","endColumn","text"}]` placed as the diagnostic
  is, and each absent rather than empty: `fix`, the rewrite that removes the
  diagnostic and keeps the program's meaning, which `nish --fix` applies; and
  then `review`, printed after `fix` (WP33 R5), on a portability warning whose
  rewrite makes the site read the same under Node and compiles to the same IR
  byte for byte, but changes what the source says, so a person or an agent
  decides: `nish --fix` never applies it. Which rows carry one is the
  portability table's last column. The
  bands and the registry are in
  [wp10-ci.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp10-ci.md#code). A clean compile with no warnings prints
  nothing.
- **`--emit-ast`** prints the syntax tree of every module after Phase 0 as an
  indented `<KIND> <start> <end>` tree — the node kinds of `src/nodes.ts` and
  each node's span as byte offsets, identifier and literal text appended — and
  writes no IR (`tests/cases/dump_ast`).
- **`--emit-checked`** checks the program and prints the side tables the
  emitter would consume: per module its structs (fields with index and byte
  offset, size, align, constructor and methods), imports, and functions
  (resolved signature, LLVM symbol, attribute facts, pointer-parameter facts,
  locals with types, callees) (`tests/cases/dump_checked`).
- **`--emit-panics <file.json>`** writes every panic site of the program,
  function by function, beside the IR, and changes no byte of it; see
  [Panic sites](#panic-sites) below.
- **`--deny-retention`** refuses a program whose own code keeps arena memory
  that nothing can reach, for a long-running program that cannot afford it; see
  [Retention as an error](#retention-as-an-error) below.
- **`--compat`** selects the compatibility dialect. It is a dialect flag, not
  a diagnostic one, and it accepts nothing yet: every rule of this document
  holds under it, a program that compiles emits the same bytes of IR with it
  as without, and a program that is refused is refused with the same exit
  status, code and message. The flag takes no value: `--compat=<anything>` is
  a usage error (exit 2). The invariant outlives this stage: a later
  `--compat` may accept a program the strict dialect refuses, and may never
  change the answer for one it does not
  (`tests/compat-erasure.js`, over every program in `tests/cases`).
- **`--emit-arena <file.json>`** writes every allocation site of the program
  with where its memory goes, beside the IR, and changes no byte of it; see
  [Arena placement](#arena-placement) below.
- **`--explain-memory`** prints, beside the warnings, every loop and function
  of the program's own modules that keeps the memory it allocates past its
  scope, and why, and changes no byte of the IR; see
  [Explaining kept memory](#explaining-kept-memory) below.
- **`-g`** emits DWARF metadata: a `DICompileUnit` (`DW_LANG_C99`) and a
  `DIFile` per source file a declaration comes from — the name as it was given
  on the command line, with `.` for the directory, so the metadata depends only
  on the command line and not on where the build ran — a `DISubprogram` per
  function, a `DILocation` on every instruction (each statement's and
  expression's start; the function's own position for the prologue),
  `llvm.dbg.value` for parameters and
  `llvm.dbg.declare` for `let`/`const` slots. `number` is `int`, `i64`
  `long`, `f64` `double`, `boolean` `bool`, `string` `char*`, a class or
  interface a pointer to a `DICompositeType` with the checker's layout, `T[]`
  a pointer to `{ long len; long cap; T* data; }`. A function's own position —
  its `DISubprogram`'s `line` and `scopeLine`, its parameters'
  `DILocalVariable`s and the `DILocation` the prologue carries — is where its
  **declaration** starts, which is the `export` or the `const` and never the
  arrow's parameter list, so the two spellings of one function describe it
  identically (`tests/cases/dbg_arrow`). A `DILocation` column is a 1-based
  **byte** offset into its line, as `clang -g` writes it, so a position after a
  multi-byte character is counted in bytes and not in UTF-16 code units
  (`tests/cases/dbg_utf8`). Without `-g` the IR is
  byte-identical. `--link -g` passes `-g` to `scripts/build.sh`, which
  compiles `runtime.c` with `-g` and skips the strip step of every profile
  (`tests/cases/dbg_locals`; the `-g` block of `tests/run.js` checks the
  linked binary's line table with `llvm-dwarfdump`).

## Writing the program out as TypeScript

- **`--emit-ts <dir>` writes the checked program back out as TypeScript**
  that Node runs with its type stripping ([wp33](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §3),
  one file per module, and emits no IR (`src/emit-ts.ts`). Each module of the
  root package keeps its path relative to the directory they all share; each
  standard-library module the program reaches is written under `nish/` beside
  them (`std/pair.ts` as `nish/pair.ts`); a dependency package's module is not
  written. Last comes `entry.ts`, which imports `nish/runtime/node`, calls
  `main` and exits with what it answered. Imports are rewritten to match: a
  `nish:` specifier becomes `nish/runtime`, the one package the output names,
  `nish:secret` included (its `std/secret.ts` is not written: the runtime's
  `wipe` answers it, a zero-fill that cannot reach a copy the engine made, so
  erasure is the native build's alone: `docs/security/secret.md`, SECRET-6),
  save `nish:async`, which becomes `nish/runtime/async.mjs` because
  `nish:process` has a `spawn` of its own in `nish/runtime`; a `nish/x` or relative one becomes the relative path, with its `.ts`; and an
  imported name that is only a type (an interface, a generic interface, an
  alias) is written `type X`, because Node's type stripping does not know
  which names are types. A module that needs none of that and none of the rows
  below is written byte for byte (`tests/emit-ts/identity/`; the layout is
  `tests/emit-ts/layout/`); one row that touches an otherwise untouched module
  is the `: string` on an unannotated `const` bound to a string literal.
- **The flag turns `--warn-portability` on**: those warnings name the sites
  where the TypeScript reading answers differently.
- **Seven kinds of module are refused, and then nothing is written** (exit 1):
  one that declares C functions, whose bodies are not in the program
  (NL4010, `tests/cases/reject_emit_ts_ffi`), and one that imports `nish:net`
  or calls a `nish:net` function, `signalFd` or `readSignal`, imported or by
  its global name, whose translation is not local to its statement (NL4011,
  `reject_emit_ts_net`, `reject_emit_ts_net_global`, `reject_emit_ts_signal`),
  and one with an `x op= e` the TypeScript writes as `x = x op e` (a width
  that wraps, a checked i32 operation, an integer `/`) whose target's index
  holds a call, a step or an element read, which would then run twice
  (NL4012, `reject_emit_ts_compound`). An index of names, their fields
  (`seen.length`), literals and their arithmetic is repeated, and `pts[i + 1].n += 10` is translated.
  The fourth is a generic whose instances would be written as different
  TypeScript, which is written once for them all: an element held inline in
  one instance and by reference in another (`P` and `P | null`), or element
  types with different zeros in `new Array<T>(n)` (`i32` and `i64`) (NL4013,
  `reject_emit_ts_instances`). Write a function per element type.
  A generic no instance reaches (a function, a method, or the methods and
  constructor of a class no type argument list names) has no types and no
  native body. Where no type would change its text it is written as it is,
  through the rewrites that need no type (`a[i]` is still checked); where a
  type would (a 64-bit integer, which is a `bigint` there, `f32`, a builtin
  call, arithmetic whose width wraps, a string's `.length` or methods, a
  `Result`'s), it is written with a body that throws. Such a stub in the
  program's own modules is a portability warning naming it at its
  declaration (NL8012, `tests/emit-ts/records/generic-uncalled.ts`); the
  standard library's (`insertAt` of `nish/collections`) are written without
  one. The fifth refusal is such a generic in the program's own modules whose
  body copies an element into an array slot, in a module that holds records
  inline, or fills `new Array<T>(n)` with `T`'s zero, which only an instance
  would decide, whatever else in it needs a type, a 64-bit integer or a
  builtin call included (NL4014, `tests/emit-ts/refused/uncalled-zero.ts`,
  `uncalled-copy.ts`, `uncalled-ctor-zero.ts`, `uncalled-field-zero.ts`,
  `uncalled-wide-zero.ts`); in the standard library the same body is a stub,
  without a warning, and the program is written. The sixth is a module that
  imports `nish:region`, whose regions the runtime the output imports
  (`nish/runtime`) does not answer yet, though a program run under Node as it
  is written does (NL4015, `reject_emit_ts_region`); keep it native.
  Every refusal in the program is reported before it exits.
- **It answers in place of the other outputs.** `--link`, `--emit-ast`,
  `--emit-checked` and the `--emit-header`/`--emit-dts`/`--emit-napi`/
  `--emit-napi-async` sidecars are refused beside it with exit 2, and so is
  `-o`, once the program is known to be writable. `--emit-ts` without a
  directory is exit 2 as well, and so is a program that cannot be laid out
  under one directory: a module above the directory of the others, or two
  modules (or one and `entry.ts`) that would be written to one path, and so
  is a directory where a file it would write is one of the program's own
  modules (`--emit-ts .` beside the sources), checked before anything is
  written.

## Panic sites

A compiled program can stop with exit 1 in more places than the `panic` calls
its author wrote: a bounds check the checker could not prove away, an integer
division, a value entering a range, `r.expect`, a `readFileSync` of a file that
is not there. Each such place is a **panic site**, and
`--emit-panics <file.json>` lists them all, per function, after the checker's
whole-program proofs have run. A site is listed exactly where the emitter
writes a check that can fail or calls into the runtime where it exits; it is
`"proven": true` where a proof table lets the emitter leave the check out, and
a function whose sites are all proven (or `oom`) has no panic path in its IR
— `npm test` holds every golden in `tests/cases/` and `tests/link/` to that
(`tests/panics-oracle.js`). The kinds:

**`index`**: `a[i]`, read or written, and `s.charCodeAt(i)`: `i` outside
`[0, length)`; and the second check of a compound store `a[i] += f()` whose
right side may resize the array

- *What proves it away:* the bounds proof of [Element
  access](expressions.md#element-access): a dominating guard, a loop bounded by the length,
  or every call site proving the argument (`tests/cases/panics_index`);
  nothing removes the second check of a compound store, which is made after
  the call however the first was proved (`tests/cases/panics_index_recheck`)

**`pop`**: `a.pop()` on an empty array

- *What proves it away:* a dominating `if (a.length > 0)`, the length fact the
  bounds proof already keeps (`tests/cases/panics_pop`)

**`slice`**: `s.slice(a, b)`, `dst.set(src, at)`,
`String.fromBytes(bytes, start, end)` and the buffer range of `netRead`,
`netWrite`, `netWrite2`, `writeBytes`, `udpSendTo` and `udpRecvFrom`: the
range outside the receiver

- *What proves it away:* nothing yet: `substring` clamps instead, and is not a
  site; an array's `xs.slice` is not a `slice` site but a `call` reaching
  `std/array.ts`'s `panic` ([Callback methods and
  `slice`](builtins.md#callback-methods-and-slice)) (`tests/cases/panics_slice`,
  `str_from_bytes_oob`, `reject_deny_panics_from_bytes`,
  `io_write_bytes_bounds`, `net_write2_bounds`)

**`divide`**: integer `/`, `%`, `/=` and `%=`: a zero divisor, or `MIN / -1`
when signed

- *What proves it away:* a divisor that is not 0, and not -1 unless the
  dividend is known non-negative: a constant (`a / 2`, `a % -3`, a folded
  module constant), a ranged or unsigned divisor whose declared range leaves
  those values out, or a guard on a local divisor —
  `if (d !== 0 && d !== -1)`, `if (d > 0)`, or `if (d !== 0)` on an unsigned
  one. A float division is not a site (`tests/cases/panics_divide`)

**`overflow`**: a signed `i32`/`i64` `+`, `-`, `*`, unary `-`, `++`, `--` or
`op=` whose result does not fit: `attempt to add with overflow` and its
siblings

- *What proves it away:* the overflow proof of [Semantics
  decisions](#semantics-decisions): an operation the bounds walk proves fits
  is `nsw` with no check (`tests/cases/panics_overflow_proven`); every other
  one is checked (`tests/cases/panics_overflow`). A `nish:unsafe`
  `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub` or `wrappingMul` is checked nowhere and is not
  a site

**`range`**: a value entering `integer<Lo, Hi>`, the store of `+=` or `++`
into a ranged place, and an exported function's check of a ranged parameter on
entry

- *What proves it away:* the range proof of
  [wp31-ranged-integers.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp31-ranged-integers.md) §8 ([Types](types.md)): a
  dominating guard such as `if (n >= 0 && n <= 9)`, or every call site proving
  the argument (`tests/cases/panics_range`)

**`array-length`**: `new Array<T>(n)` whose length type could make a bad
header or a negative byte count (an `i64`, a float, an `i32` or a ranged
integer, a `u32` under `--number-mode i32`)

- *What proves it away:* a narrower unsigned length or a literal up to 2^31 -
  1, which is not checked and not a site (`tests/cases/panics_array_length`)

**`panic`**: `panic(message)`

- *What proves it away:* nothing: a path the program never takes is still a
  site (`tests/cases/panics_panic`)

**`expect`**: `r.expect(message)` on an `Err`

- *What proves it away:* nothing; `unwrapOr` and `orReturn` are not sites
  (`tests/cases/panics_expect`)

**`io-exit`**: `readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`, `appendFileSync` and
`crypto.getRandomValues`, which exit inside the runtime on failure

- *What proves it away:* nothing; `readFileSyncOrNull` is the twin that
  answers `null` instead (`tests/cases/panics_io_exit`)

**`parallel-length`**: a `parallelMapInto` call whose `dst` is shorter than
its `src`

- *What proves it away:* nothing yet: the check is `std/threads.ts`'s own
  (`tests/link/panics_parallel_length`)

**`ffi-nul`**: a `string` argument to a [`declare function`](declarations.md#calling-c) that
holds a NUL byte, which C would read as the end of the string:
`` `name`: argument N (param) holds a NUL byte, which C would read as the end of the string ``

- *What proves it away:* a literal with no NUL in it, which is not checked and
  not a site; every other string is checked, and `string | null` checks only
  the string (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_nul`)

**`ffi-null`**: a `string` result of a [`declare function`](declarations.md#calling-c) that
is `NULL`:
`` `name` returned NULL for a `string` result; declare it `string | null` ``;
or the pointer of a [`readStruct`](declarations.md#readstruct-a-struct-out-of-memory-c-owns)
call that is `NULL`: `` `readStruct` read a NULL pointer into a `Lconv` ``;
or the pointer of a
[`readCString`](declarations.md#readcstring-a-string-out-of-a-buffer-c-owns) call that is
`NULL`: `` `readCString` read a NULL pointer ``

- *What proves it away:* nothing: a result declared `string | null` reads
  `NULL` as `null` and is not a site (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_null`); the
  `readStruct` and `readCString` tests stay at every call
  (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_read_struct_null`,
  `tests/cases/panics_ffi_read_cstring_null`)

**`ffi-length`**: a call to a
[`declare function`](declarations.md#a-u8-parameter-a-buffer-and-its-count) whose count is
larger than a `u8[]` buffer of its run:
`` `name`: argument N (count) counts more bytes than argument M (buf) holds ``,
compared unsigned, so a count that wrapped below zero fails too

- *What proves it away:* a count of `toU64(b.length)` where `b` is that buffer
  itself, a `const` local or a parameter named alone, and no later argument
  may resize an array (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_count_proved`,
  `ffi_buffer_late_load`); every other count is checked
  (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_length`, `panics_ffi_length_wrapped`,
  `panics_ffi_length_shrink`).

**`region`**: a call to `nish:region`'s `region`, `regionWith`, `enter`,
`enterWith` or `free`: a handle that is 0, freed, another thread's or entered
already, a `free` of an entered region, or more live regions than the table
holds

- *What proves it away:* nothing: the handle is a number the checker does not
  follow, so every call checks it (`tests/cases/reject_deny_panics_region`)

**`call`**: a call into a function that has a site that can panic, directly or
through further calls

- *What proves it away:* the callee having none (`tests/cases/panics_call`)

**`unchecked`**: `uncheckedGet` and `uncheckedSet` from `nish:unsafe`: no
check at all, so nothing panics, but an index out of range is undefined
behaviour (`readCString` and `readStruct` test their pointer for `NULL`, so
each is an `ffi-null` site above)

- *What proves it away:* nothing, and nothing needs to: the call is the
  author's word that the index is in range, not a
  proof, and the `nish:unsafe` import its module must write is the opt-in to
  that word, so it is listed with `"allowed": true` and, like `oom`, never
  makes a function one that may panic (`tests/cases/deny_panics_unsafe`)

**`oom`**: an arena allocation: the out-of-memory exit

- *What proves it away:* nothing, and nothing needs to: it is listed with
  `"allowed": true` and never makes a function one that may panic
  (`tests/cases/panics_oom`)

- **A `call` names its callee and the kind it reaches** (`"via"`), and is
  decided over the whole program, the standard library and dependencies
  included. The kind is the one the callee reaches first at run time, its own
  checks and its calls taken together: an operation checks its operands once
  they are evaluated, so `pick(xs, i) + 1`, `1 + pick(xs, i)`,
  `x += pick(xs, i)` and `100 / pick(xs, i)` reach `pick`'s `index` before
  their own `overflow` or `divide`, while `pick(xs, i - 1)` reaches its
  argument's `overflow` before the call (`tests/cases/panics_overflow_via`).
  In a cycle of calls made before any check, the cycle's first function in
  declaration order with a site of its own or a call out of the cycle passes
  over its calls back into it, and the rest of the cycle reaches what it
  reaches (`tests/cases/panics_call_cycle`). The list itself stays in source
  order, by where each site starts. A generic function's sites are its instantiations', each under its
  own symbol and decided over its own side tables
  (`tests/cases/panics_generic`).
- **Two ways a program can stop are not sites**, because no proof the checker
  makes could remove them. Out of memory is listed, as `oom`, but excluded: every
  allocation can fail and no guard in the source prevents it. Stack overflow is
  a fault the operating system raises, with no handler in the runtime and no
  check in the IR. Signed overflow is a site, `overflow`, because it is checked
  (see *Signed integer overflow is a checked panic* above). Neither are
  `process.exit(n)`, which is a deliberate exit, or a call into a `declare
  function`, whose body is C the compiler does not see.
- **The file is a contract**, like `--json`: one `{"functions":[...]}` object,
  one function per line in module and declaration order, each
  `{"name","symbol","module","line","panics"}`, where `symbol` is the
  function's LLVM name; per site `{"kind","line","column"}` and then
  `"proven"` for a check, `"proven","callee"` for `parallel-length`,
  `"callee","via"` for `call` and `"allowed": true` for `oom` and `unchecked`. Lines and
  columns are 1-based, in the units a diagnostic uses. The `wrote <file>` line
  is on stderr, like the IR's. It is written once the program is checked: a
  program that does not compile writes none, and `--emit-checked` writes it
  beside its dump. `--emit-ast`, which stops before the check, refuses it with
  a usage error (exit 2) rather than leaving the file unwritten, and so do
  `nish run`, which keeps its build to itself, and `--fix`, which writes no IR.

## The no-panic scope

A module can be **required** to have no panic site left. `--deny-panics` puts
every module of the program's own package in the scope; the root package's
`package.json` — the one nearest above the entry file — puts the modules it
lists there, by their path relative to that file:

```json
{ "nish": { "noPanic": ["src/parser.ts", "src/lexer.ts"] } }
```

Both together put the union in scope; with neither, nothing changes. In a
module of the scope, every site of a kind above that is not proven is an
error, NL2457, which names the kind and, where a proof the checker makes would
remove the check, the guard that gives it — the same sentence the performance
warnings use for an index (NL9007) and a range entry (NL9013), so one way of
writing each is taught (`tests/cases/reject_deny_panics_<kind>`, one per kind;
`tests/cases/deny_panics_clean` is the module that passes, and its IR has no
`nish_panic_` call and no panic tail). Where a refused site sits in a loop, the
performance warning about the same check is not printed beside the error.

- **A call out of the scope is refused at the call** (NL2458): the standard
  library and a dependency are not in the scope — their author, not this one,
  proves them — but a call from the scope into one of their functions that may
  panic names the callee and the site it reaches (`reject_deny_panics_call`,
  `tests/link/no_panic_transitive`). A call into a function that is itself in
  the scope is not refused again: its own sites are.
- **A module the list does not name keeps its checks**: the same unproven index
  is refused in a listed module and compiles in an unlisted one
  (`tests/link/no_panic_module`, `tests/link/no_panic_unlisted`).
- **An entry that names no module of the program is an error** (NL3031),
  reported in `package.json` where the entry is written: a typo would
  otherwise leave the module it meant outside the scope without a word
  (`tests/link/no_panic_unknown_entry`).
- **The root package's `"nish"` field is one object, written once, whose
  keys are `noPanic`, `capabilities` and `host`, each written once**, and anything
  else is an error (NL3036) where `package.json` writes it: a second `"nish"`
  even when neither holds a policy (`caps_policy_manifest_repeated_nish_no_panic`),
  a `"nish"` that is not an object (`caps_policy_manifest_nish_not_object`), a
  key it does not know, a misspelt `capabilites` included
  (`caps_policy_manifest_nish_unknown_key`), a `noPanic` that is not an array
  (`caps_policy_manifest_no_panic_not_array`), and a manifest that mentions
  `nish` or carries a `\u` escape and stops being JSON
  (`caps_policy_manifest_broken_json`). Each would otherwise leave part of
  what the package says about itself unread. A key is decoded as `JSON.parse`
  decodes it, so `"ni\u0073h"` is `"nish"`; an escape outside ASCII decodes
  to a byte no name contains, so it never matches one.
- **A `nish:unsafe` import is the opt-in.** `uncheckedGet` and `uncheckedSet`
  are reached only through `import { … } from "nish:unsafe"` at the top of the
  module that calls them, which is the module's word, visible where a reader
  looks first, that its indexes are in range. So the scope allows them, as
  `unchecked` sites with `"allowed": true`, and a call into a function whose
  only unproven sites are `unchecked` is not a `call` site at all, from inside
  the scope or out of it (`tests/cases/deny_panics_unsafe`,
  `tests/link/no_panic_unsafe_callee`). The global spelling `tsc` accepts has
  no import to show and is refused, scope or not (NL2456,
  `reject_deny_panics_unsafe_no_import`).
- **Signed overflow is refused where it is not proven.** Every signed `+`, `-`,
  `*`, unary `-`, `++`, `--` and `op=` the bounds walk has not proven to fit is
  an `overflow` site, refused like an index or a divisor, with a hint to bound
  its operands, compute in `u32`/`u64` (the width's unsigned type), or write
  the operator's drop-in `nish:unsafe` form: `wrappingAdd(x, y)`,
  `wrappingSub(x, y)`, `wrappingMul(x, y)`, `x = wrappingAdd(x, y)` for an
  `op=`, `wrappingSub(0, x)` for a negation and `x = wrappingAdd(x, 1)` or
  `x = wrappingSub(x, 1)` for `++` and `--`. A proven one is accepted, and so is
  every `wrapping*` call, which is defined to wrap and is not a site
  (`tests/cases/reject_deny_panics_overflow`, `tests/cases/reject_deny_panics_overflow_ops`, `tests/cases/deny_panics_overflow_proven`,
  `tests/cases/deny_panics_overflow_wrapping_add`,
  `tests/link/no_panic_overflow`).
- **What the scope does not cover.** Out of memory is listed but never
  refused: every allocation can fail and no guard prevents it. Stack overflow
  is a fault the operating system raises, with no check in the IR to refuse.
  So a module in the scope cannot *panic* except by running out of memory,
  and that is the whole claim. Nor can it reach undefined behaviour through a
  check the compiler left out, except where a `nish:unsafe` import says so.
- `--deny-panics` changes no byte of the IR: a program it accepts is the one the
  build compiles without it. With `--emit-ast`, which stops before the checker,
  it is a usage error (exit 2).

## Retention as an error

A program that runs for a long time, a server above all, cannot afford memory
that stays allocated after nothing can reach it: in a command-line tool it is
returned when `main` does, and in a server it grows until the process is
killed. Six performance warnings are exactly that finding, and
**`--deny-retention`** makes each of them an error (NL2462) in the program's own
modules:

| Warning | What stays allocated |
| --- | --- |
| NL9002, quadratic string building | every intermediate string of `s = s + t` in a loop |
| NL9003, an allocation dropped by an assignment | the value the local held |
| NL9011, a loop that leaves a callee's memory behind | what the callee left on every pass |
| NL9016, an allocation dropped on every pass | the value each pass replaced |
| NL9018, a pass of an unbounded loop that keeps what it allocates | the temporary each pass built, for as long as the loop runs |
| NL9019, a function that keeps memory on every call | what each call a loop makes keeps |

- **The error keeps the warning.** Its text is the warning's, after the code of
  the rule that found it, so it names the same rewrite:
  `` `--deny-retention` refuses this NL9016 finding, because the arena memory it describes stays allocated after nothing in the program can reach it any more: `last` is given a new allocation on every pass of this loop … ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_deny_retention_pass_drop`, `reject_deny_retention_drop`,
  `reject_deny_retention_loop`, `reject_deny_retention_concat`,
  `reject_deny_retention_unbounded_pass`, `reject_deny_retention_kept`, and for
  a `Result` assigned over another, `reject_deny_retention_result_drop` and
  `reject_deny_retention_result_reassign`). The warning it
  restates is not printed as well, and `--no-warn-performance` does not
  silence the error.
- **The program's own modules only.** A module of the root package is held to
  it; a dependency's warnings stay warnings, as its panic sites stay outside
  the [no-panic scope](#the-no-panic-scope), because the program's author
  cannot change that code (`tests/link/deny_retention_dependency`).
- **What it does not promise.** The five warnings are conservative in the
  direction of silence: each fires only where the compiler can name the memory
  and the rewrite, so a program it accepts can still retain memory in a shape
  no rule recognises ([wp6-memory.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp6-memory.md), "Left out"). Nor does it
  cover memory a program keeps on purpose: an array it pushes onto for its
  whole run is reachable, and so not retention.
- `--deny-retention` changes no byte of the IR: a program it accepts is the one
  the build compiles without it (`tests/cases/deny_retention_clean`). `nish run`
  and `--fix` accept it; with `--emit-ast`, which stops before the checker, it
  is a usage error (exit 2).

## Arena placement

**`--emit-arena <file.json>`** writes where the memory of every allocation site
goes: the decisions the [memory model](#memory-model) made, read back in the
order the emitter applies them, so the file and the IR cannot disagree. It is
the audit for the cases no warning names: a site a rule stays silent about is
still in the file, with its placement.

The file is one JSON object, one function per line, in module order and, in
each module, in declaration order followed by the instantiations of its
generic functions, and its sites in source order. The keys and their order are
a contract, like `--emit-panics`':

```
{"functions":[
{"name":"main","symbol":"nish_main","module":"tests/cases/arena_placement.ts","line":32,"sites":[{"kind":"new","line":34,"column":13,"placement":"stack"},…,{"kind":"string","line":52,"column":12,"placement":"function","accumulates":true}]}
]}
```

Per function `{"name","symbol","module","line","sites"}`, as `--emit-panics`
writes them, and a generic function once per instantiation. Per site
`{"kind","line","column","placement"}`, then `"callee"` for a `call` and a
`builtin`, then `"accumulates":true` where it applies. A site's **kind** is
`new`, `object`, `array`, `string` (a concatenation or a template), `push`,
`print` (a number `console.log` formats), `builtin` (a runtime function that
allocates, such as `join`) or `call` (a user function whose memory the result
is). Its **placement** is the first of these that holds:

| Placement | Where the memory goes |
| --- | --- |
| `stack` | an entry-block `alloca`, reused on every pass of a loop |
| `pass` | released at the end of each pass of the innermost scoped loop around it |
| `block` | released when the block of the `using a = arena()` before it ends |
| `function` | released when the function returns: its arena scope |
| `returned` | handed to the caller with the return value, whose placement decides |
| `caller` | released when the function returns, by every caller's reclaim of the returned string |
| `kept` | stored into memory older than the function, and as long-lived as it |
| `unscoped` | released by nothing in this function: it lives as long as the caller's memory, which in `main` is the rest of the run |

**`accumulates`** marks a site that runs on every pass of a loop that releases
nothing per pass — or in that loop's condition or update, which run outside
the bracket a pass takes — and whose memory is unreachable before its
release: `pass`, `block`, `function`, `caller` or `unscoped`. Its memory piles up pass
after pass until then. `` last = `item ${i}` `` in a loop over ten million
passes is a `function` site that accumulates in a `main` that earns a scope
through its callees, and an `unscoped` one in a function that has none
(`tests/cases/arena_placement`, `arena_placement_loops`). A `returned` or `kept`
site is memory the program holds on purpose, so it is never marked.

- **The answer is about the site's own function.** A scope in a caller can
  still release an `unscoped` site's memory: a loop whose pass is scoped takes
  back what its callees leave behind. Only in `main` is `unscoped` the end of
  the run.
- `--emit-arena` changes no byte of the IR, and it is a product, as
  `--emit-panics` is: `nish run` and `--fix` refuse it, and so does
  `--emit-ast`, which stops before the facts exist (exit 2).

## Explaining kept memory

**`--explain-memory`** answers, before the program is deployed, the question a
memory budget turns on: which loops hand back what each pass allocated, and
which do not. The [memory model](#memory-model) gives a pass of a loop, and a
function, an arena scope of its own when it can prove what they allocated is
unreachable at the end; one stored allocation, in the loop or in any callee,
refuses the scope, and the memory the pass allocated then stays until the next
bracket out. The warnings name such a refusal only where they can also name a
rewrite; this report names every one, on stderr, after the warnings (an
excerpt of `tests/cases/explain_memory`):

```
tests/cases/explain_memory.ts:21:1: memory: `remember` keeps what it allocates until the memory of its caller is released, because the allocation on line 22 is stored into memory, where this analysis stops following it
tests/cases/explain_memory.ts:43:20: memory: this loop's condition allocates on every pass, outside the scope a pass takes, and keeps it until `extra` returns
tests/cases/explain_memory.ts:43:40: memory: this loop's update allocates on every pass, outside the scope a pass takes, and keeps it until `extra` returns
tests/cases/explain_memory.ts:60:3: memory: this loop keeps what each pass allocates until `main` returns, because line 61 keeps what the pass allocated in `last`, which is declared outside the loop
tests/cases/explain_memory.ts:76:10: memory: this loop's condition allocates on every pass, outside the scope a pass takes, and keeps it until `main` returns
explain-memory: 7 of 9 allocating loops keep what a pass allocates past the pass; 1 of 4 allocating functions with a scalar result keep what they allocate past the call
```

- **A loop** is listed when its passes allocate — themselves, or through a
  callee that leaves memory behind — and no scope releases it at the end of
  each pass. The line says where it does go back: at the end of the pass of the
  scoped loop around it, at the end of the `using a = arena()` block around it,
  when the function returns, or, in a function with no scope, when its caller's
  memory is (in `main`, never: "for the rest of the run"). The reason is the
  first refusal the analysis met, the one NL9011 names. A loop whose every
  allocation goes back with a `using a = arena()` block or a scoped loop
  inside its body keeps nothing past the pass and is not listed. A condition or `for` update that allocates is
  listed on its own line — both, when both do — because it runs outside the
  bracket a pass takes whether or not the body has one; a `do...while`
  condition's line follows the lines of the loops in its body.
- **A listed loop with no bound** — one that is not bounded, by NL9018's rule — is
  the loop NL9018 warns about when what its pass keeps is a temporary the
  pass drops; the report lists it either way.
- **A function** is listed when it answers a number, a `boolean`, an enum or
  nothing, leaves memory behind, and has no scope of its own. A function that
  answers memory (a string, an array, an object) is not, nor is a constructor,
  which answers the object it builds: what it allocates goes to its caller with
  the result, and whether the caller gives it back is the
  caller's line.
- **The summary** counts the loops whose passes allocate and the functions that
  answer no memory and allocate, and how many of each keep it. A budget in CI
  can hold that count, or the listed lines, against a golden, as
  `tests/run.js` does with a case's `<name>.memory`
  (`tests/cases/explain_memory`).
- **The program's own modules only**, as `--deny-retention` judges them. A
  generic function, or one that takes a function parameter, is explained once
  per instantiation, under its instantiated name (`` `each<twice>` ``), after
  the functions declared outright (`tests/cases/explain_memory_calls`).
- **A callee the analysis cannot see counts as allocating.** In a function
  that allocates, a loop with no scope that calls one is listed, since nothing
  proves its passes leave no memory behind. A function that allocates nothing
  the analysis can see is not examined.
- **A callee's leak is its caller's.** A function whose kept allocation is a
  call names that callee. One whose own allocation is held where the analysis
  does not prove it dead names that first, whatever its callees do. One that
  keeps memory only because a function down its calls holds an allocation the
  analysis does not prove dead names that function, the one the doubt starts
  in, even when that function's own scope gives its memory back: the doubt
  passes up every call.
- **A function is judged by what it still holds when it returns.** One with
  no scope of its own keeps nothing when every allocation it leaves is inside
  a scoped pass or a `using a = arena()` block, so it is counted and not
  listed; one that is listed names the line of the first allocation it holds.
- **Under `--no-elision`** no automatic scope is taken, so every allocating
  loop and function is listed except the passes and blocks the program
  brackets itself with `using a = arena()`.
- **What it does not promise.** It reports the scopes the compiler takes, not
  the bytes: a listed loop over three passes costs nothing, and memory the
  program keeps on purpose — an array it pushes onto for its whole run — is
  listed with the line that keeps it. It does not measure memory at run time.
- `--explain-memory` changes no byte of the IR. `nish run` accepts it. A build
  refused after the analysis has run (by `--deny-retention`, or a check that
  follows it) still prints the report after the errors, since it says why each
  refused loop keeps its memory; one refused earlier prints none. With
  `--emit-ast`, which stops before the facts exist, with `--json`, whose
  stderr is diagnostic objects only, and with `--fix`, which compiles nothing,
  it is a usage error (exit 2).
